walkthroughs.body_html:
Environmental & Ecological Economics — a core area of Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Environmental & Ecological Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Environmental & Ecological Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Why are invasive species often more harmful than native species?
options: Cold winters are caused by warming.
They lack natural predators or competitors in their new environment, so they spread unchecked.
They are larger than native species.
They are inherently more aggressive than native species.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?
options: One is for plants, the other for animals.
They are larger than native species.
They are alternative names for the same approach.
In-situ protects species in their natural habitat; ex-situ removes them to controlled settings like zoos or seed banks.

mcqs.q: Why is a cold winter not evidence against climate change?
options: Cold winters are caused by warming.
It is evidence - if it gets cold sometimes, warming must be wrong.
One is for plants, the other for animals.
Climate refers to long-term averages, not individual weather events.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Earth Summit”?
options: Worldview shaping how individuals/societies evaluate environmental issues; ecocentric, anthropocentric, technocentric (IBDP categorisation).
Analysing environment as interlinked open systems with inputs, outputs, flows, feedbacks.
Individual rational use of shared resource leads to collective ruin (Hardin 1968 in Science).
1992 Rio Conference produced Agenda 21, UNFCCC and CBD; landmark in environmental governance.

Meeting present needs without compromising ability of future generations to meet theirs (Brundtland 1987).
